proposal.utterance: Classify 'Abusus' (the right of abuse, in Roman-law property theory) in BFO terms.

entities.label: Abusus
entities.rationale: Abusus (ius abutendi) is the right to dispose of or alienate a thing — one of the three classical sticks in the Roman dominium bundle (usus, fructus, abusus). As a legal right, it is a role-type: it is externally grounded in a legal system's recognition of the owner's entitlement, it inheres in a bearer (the owner/legal person), and it is realized in acts of disposal or alienation. It is therefore a subclass of working:LegalRight, which is itself typed as BFO_0000023 (Role). Modeling as a class rather than an individual because 'Abusus' names a kind of legal entitlement, not a particular token right held by a specific person.

entities.label: ActOfDisposal
entities.rationale: Abusus is realized in acts of alienating, destroying, or otherwise disposing of a thing. BFO roles are realized in processes (BFO_0000054 realized in). ActOfDisposal is the process class in which instances of Abusus are realized. It is a subclass of BFO Process.

entities.label: DominiumBundle
entities.rationale: Roman dominium is the full property right, composed of usus, fructus, and abusus. It is usefully modeled as a role-class whose instances have Abusus (and the other sticks) as parts. Typing as a class subsuming working:LegalRight (BFO_0000023). This allows the part-of structure among the component rights to be expressed.

relations.rationale: Abusus is a specific kind of LegalRight, itself typed as BFO_0000023 Role; subclass relation captures this specialization.
Instances of the Abusus role are realized in instances of ActOfDisposal processes, per BFO's realized-in relation (BFO_0000054).
Abusus is one component (part) of the full Roman dominium bundle of rights; BFO_0000050 (part of) captures the mereological relation between the specific stick and the whole bundle at the type level.
ActOfDisposal is a kind of process (BFO_0000015).
DominiumBundle is a composite kind of LegalRight.

open_questions: Should Abusus be modeled as a Disposition (BFO_0000016) rather than a Role (BFO_0000023)? Roles are externally grounded (in social/legal recognition), while Dispositions are internally grounded. For a legal right like Abusus, external legal recognition grounds it, favoring Role — but some theorists treat property entitlements as legally conferred capacities, which could favor Disposition. Which framing does the user prefer?
Should 'usus' (right of use) and 'fructus' (right to fruits) also be minted as sibling classes of Abusus under DominiumBundle, to complete the Roman property triad?
Is DominiumBundle intended to cover only Roman-law property, or should it be a general 'BundleOfRights' class applicable to modern property theory as well (e.g., Honoré's incidents of ownership)?
Should ActOfDisposal be further subdivided into ActOfAlienation (transfer to another) and ActOfDestruction (physical destruction), given that Roman abusus encompasses both?
proposal.rationale_summary: Abusus (ius abutendi) is the Roman-law entitlement to alienate or destroy a thing — the 'disposal stick' in the dominium bundle. In BFO terms it is most naturally a Role (BFO_0000023): it is a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in a legal person (the owner), is externally grounded in Roman/civil-law recognition, and is realized in concrete acts of disposal or alienation. It is modeled as a class (a kind of entitlement) rather than an individual, because 'Abusus' names a universally instantiated right-type. It is placed as a subclass of the existing working:LegalRight (which is already typed BFO_0000023). Two supporting classes are proposed: ActOfDisposal (BFO_0000015 Process), the process type in which Abusus is realized, and DominiumBundle (also a LegalRight subclass), representing the composite Roman property right of which Abusus is a mereological part. Key open questions concern whether Disposition rather than Role is the better BFO home, and whether the full usus/fructus/abusus triad should be modeled symmetrically.
